title: Evaluation & Guardrails

character.name: The Gatekeeper
character.tagline: Nothing ships past me without proof it actually works.

oneLiner: How do you know your AI is good — and keep it safe? Evals, LLM-as-judge, and guardrails.
analogy: Shipping an AI feature without evals is like launching a restaurant without ever tasting the food — you'll find out it's bad from the reviews (angry users). Evals are your tasting menu: a fixed set of test cases you run every time you change a prompt or model, scoring whether outputs are correct, safe, and on-format. Since grading thousands of free-text answers by hand is brutal, you often enlist another LLM as a judge. Guardrails are the bouncers at the door and exit: blocking toxic inputs, filtering unsafe outputs, and catching hallucinations before users see them.
objectives: Understand why systematic evaluation is essential for AI features.
Build eval sets and use metrics/rubrics (incl. LLM-as-judge).
Apply guardrails for input/output safety and format validation.
Detect and mitigate hallucinations in production.
keyConcepts: Evals are repeatable test suites (inputs + expected qualities) you run whenever prompts, models, or pipelines change — your regression tests for AI.
Because outputs are open-ended, you evaluate with rubrics, reference answers, or an 'LLM-as-judge' scoring responses against criteria.
Guardrails validate and filter: block unsafe/off-topic inputs, check outputs for safety, PII, or policy violations, and enforce output formats.
Hallucination mitigation includes grounding (RAG), asking for citations, and verification/second-pass checks.
Track quality with real metrics (accuracy on evals, pass rates, user feedback) rather than vibes.
'Offline' evals (before release) and 'online' monitoring (in production) are both needed.

keyTerms.plain: A test suite for your AI — run it every time you change something.
Using another model to grade open-ended answers against a rubric.
A safety filter on what goes in and what comes out.
When a 'small' prompt tweak quietly breaks other cases.
A trusted set of examples with known-good answers for testing.

scenarios.scenario: You tweak a prompt to fix one bad case. It works — but you're worried the change quietly broke other cases you can't check by hand.
scenarios.question: What practice prevents this?

options.label: Maintain an eval set and run it on every change to catch regressions
Ship and wait for user complaints
Only test the one case you just fixed

scenarios.explanation: An eval suite acts like regression tests: running it on every prompt/model change reveals whether a fix broke other cases, before users do.

scenarios.scenario: You must grade 5,000 open-ended summaries for quality, and manual review is infeasible.
scenarios.question: Which scalable evaluation approach is appropriate?

options.label: LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric, spot-checked against human ratings
Only exact string matching to a single reference

scenarios.explanation: For open-ended outputs at scale, an LLM-as-judge with a well-defined rubric (validated against some human labels) is a practical way to evaluate quality.

quiz.question: What are 'evals' in AI engineering?
options: Repeatable test suites that measure output quality when prompts/models/pipelines change
quiz.answer: Repeatable test suites that measure output quality when prompts/models/pipelines change
quiz.explanation: Evals are like regression tests for AI: run them on every change to ensure quality doesn't silently degrade.

quiz.question: 'LLM-as-judge' refers to:
options: Using an LLM to score open-ended outputs against defined criteria/rubrics
A way to train the base model
quiz.answer: Using an LLM to score open-ended outputs against defined criteria/rubrics
quiz.explanation: When outputs are free-form and manual grading doesn't scale, an LLM can evaluate responses against a rubric (ideally validated against human judgments).

quiz.question: Guardrails are used to:
options: Validate/filter inputs and outputs for safety, policy, PII, and format
quiz.answer: Validate/filter inputs and outputs for safety, policy, PII, and format
quiz.explanation: Guardrails check what goes in and comes out — blocking unsafe content, protecting sensitive data, and enforcing required formats.

quiz.question: Which technique helps reduce hallucinations in production?
options: Grounding answers with RAG and requesting citations/verification
quiz.answer: Grounding answers with RAG and requesting citations/verification
quiz.explanation: Grounding in retrieved sources, asking for citations, and adding verification steps all reduce (not eliminate) hallucinations.

quiz.question: Why isn't 'it looked good in a demo' enough to ship an AI feature?
options: A few good examples don't prove consistent quality/safety across many real inputs; systematic evals do
quiz.answer: A few good examples don't prove consistent quality/safety across many real inputs; systematic evals do
quiz.explanation: Anecdotes aren't evidence of reliability. Evals and monitoring provide measurable confidence across the range of real inputs.
